text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Tuesday.

GERMANY - German Bunds and futures retained their firm undertone in late dealings on Tuesday after a volatile trading session where various central bankers battled for the markets' attention. The December Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 98.13, up 0.17 from Monday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilt futures ended with small losses on Tuesday as fears of a U.S. interest rate rise next week put bond markets on the back foot, dealers said. The December long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 107-27/32, down 02/32 from Monday's settlement price.

FRANCE - French bond futures slipped from a new contract high set earlier in the session after fears of a U.S. rate rise next week sent U.S. bond prices lower. The December notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 124.06 up 0.20 from Monday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian debt markets shadowed other bond markets to end a choppy day's trade between 10 and 20 basis points higher. The December bond future on LIFFE was trading at 117.94 up 0.20 from Monday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - Prices of U.S. Treasury securities were stuck at substantially lower levels near midday after comments from a senior Fed official aggravated fears of a rate hike and sent prices south, analysts said. The December Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 108-06/32, down 20/32 from Monday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 7.0 percent.

JAPAN - The key December Japanese government bond (JGB) futures contract soared to end near a nine-month high (corrects) in active trade on Tuesday. In after hours trading the December future on LIFFE was trading at 121.98, up 0.20 from Monday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
EUROBONDS - The dollar sector provided the main interest on Tuesday, with a number of expected deals coming to the market.
Ford Motor Credit Co launched a $1.0 billion five-year global bond via Goldman Sachs which will be priced to yield between 48 and 50 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes.
Feedback on the deal was positive, with traders reporting strong interest from both U.S. and non-U.S. accounts.
The pricing was considered "spot-on", with the yield a couple of basis points higher than that available in the secondary market.
